slides.title: AI in audit & assurance
slides.note: Introduce the next section: AI in audit & assurance. What changes when AI becomes part of assurance?

slides.title: Two roles for AI in supervision
slides.note: Bridge before the technical detail. Mengawasi AI means examining AI as a source of risk: intended use, data, validation, fairness, security, access, monitoring, vendor dependencies and a named accountable owner. Mengawasi dengan AI means using AI to assist oversight of activities and risks, including activities that do not use AI. These are complementary roles, not interchangeable terms. An AI supervisory tool itself belongs within AI governance. The next two slides explain the three layers of frontier AI risk and the scope of AI oversight before returning to SupTech.

links.label: OECD / Supervision of Artificial Intelligence in Finance (2026) ↗

slides.title: Three layers of frontier AI risk
slides.note: Source: presenter-supplied Understanding Frontier AI - IHT OJK 2026.pptx, displayed slide 26 / 64, Tiga layer risiko frontier AI. This training taxonomy distinguishes model behavior, malicious use of capabilities, and deployment or shared-dependency risk. The layers can overlap: a prompt-injection attack is malicious use that exploits the deployed system. Herding refers to correlated behavior when institutions rely on similar models or signals. This slide explains why AI is an object of oversight. Next: examine purpose, accountability, data, authority and monitoring across the system.

slides.title: Supervise AI: what must we examine?
slides.note: Source: presenter-supplied Understanding Frontier AI - IHT OJK 2026.pptx, displayed slides 48-50 / 64. This is a training synthesis, not a regulatory checklist. Human-in-the-loop: a person approves each consequential decision. Human-on-the-loop: a person monitors and can override within defined limits. Human-in-command: people set the permitted autonomy, guardrails and stop conditions; this can coexist with the other arrangements. The use-case owner owns outcomes and controls, risk/compliance challenges and monitors, and internal audit independently assesses governance and control effectiveness. Examine the deployed system, including vendor components, rather than model accuracy alone. Transition: AI used for supervision also needs this oversight. Continue to SupTech.

slides.title: SupTech: from more data to focused supervision
slides.note: Pengawasan menggunakan AI is an AI-enabled part of SupTech, not the definition of all SupTech. Financial authorities use the term for technology supporting supervision, including data collection and analytics; the organizational example here is an illustrative adaptation, not a regulatory classification. Potential uses include document extraction, anomaly detection, thematic analysis and prioritization. Outputs support rather than replace supervisory judgment: a flag is not proof of a violation or an automatic risk-score change. Require traceable sources, permitted data access, validation and monitoring of false positives and missed signals. Transition: what objectives, risks and controls give these signals meaning? That leads into performance, risk and assurance. SIGNAL demonstrates this decision workflow with transparent rules; no language model is connected.

slides.title: SupTech in practice: authorities using AI
slides.note: Use this concrete bridge after the SupTech introduction and before narrowing to risk management. ECB is the authority for European banking supervision, not the European Union as a single national regulator. Its November 2023 account describes Athena and Heimdall among live tools; do not infer that later LLM features were already operational then. PRA cognitive search is described as successfully introduced in Box 3 of DP5/22 (2022). FINMA describes its local GenAI pre-inspection tool as a proof of concept in June 2026, so do not present it as a fully deployed supervisory system. These examples establish actual authority practice and experimentation, not evidence that AI makes autonomous supervisory decisions. The supplied reference image guides the comparative card format; unverified claims and its survey statistic are not reproduced.

slides.title: Our use case: AI for risk management
slides.note: This is the scope-setting bridge: we have introduced the two roles of AI and the broader SupTech concept; now we narrow to a risk-management use case. This is an organizational adaptation of the supervisory logic, not a claim that all risk management is formally classified as SupTech. AI would assist evidence capture, relevance screening and review suggestions. The accountable risk owner decides whether to capture a signal, whether the assessment should change and which response to own. Assurance provides evidence on controls and response effectiveness. The workshop demonstrates that workflow using transparent rules; it does not connect to a live language model. Transition to the next slide: to make this work, we need to connect performance, risk and assurance around the same objective.

slides.title: Rethink risk management.
slides.note: Introduce the next section: The disconnect. Does evidence change the next management decision?

slides.title: AI can assist the whole risk cycle.
slides.note: AI can assist identification, assessment, treatment and monitoring: reading context, drafting risks, bringing evidence together, proposing scores and responses, and watching change. This is a capability argument, not a claim that the deployed seminar app uses a language model. Human review is mandatory at each material judgment: validate evidence and relevance, authorize the assessment and response, assign ownership, and verify effectiveness. Autonomy must remain within explicitly approved boundaries. The next slide distinguishes task automation from the organizational integration needed to protect objectives.

slides.title: Better tools. Still disconnected?
slides.note: AI can improve individual tasks without fixing disconnected performance, risk and assurance processes. The meaningful test is whether evidence changes a forecast, assessment or owned response in time to protect the objective. This bridges the broad AI risk-cycle capability to the three disciplines and their practical handoffs, then to the SIGNAL framework. This is a design proposition and diagnostic question, not a measured universal failure rate.

slides.title: Three disciplines. One purpose.
slides.note: These are three connected GRC disciplines selected for this seminar, not the expansion of the GRC acronym or an exhaustive list. Compliance and integrity remain foundational. Definitions are concise paraphrases: OCEG connects disciplines; COSO integrates risk with strategy and performance; the IIA distinguishes management responsibility from independent assurance. Balanced Scorecard and KPI practices operationalize performance; no claim that the three are a formal new standard.

slides.title: Can evidence cross the boundaries?
slides.note: Read left to right: objective, exposure, confidence in protection. Ask participants for the last occasion an audit finding changed a risk assessment and an action protecting a KPI. These questions diagnose practice; they do not establish that every Kemenkeu unit is disconnected.

slides.title: Shared goals. Disconnected decisions?
slides.note: The moving paths represent the recurring exchange that should take place, not evidence that it already does. Static callouts stay attached to the two relationships. The evidence loop starts automatically; pause it to discuss a relationship. Leaving the slide stops it. The pain point is a weak evidence-to-decision handoff, rather than the absence of systems or professional effort.

slides.title: 89% did not report a unique strategic advantage.
slides.note: Read the displayed response level precisely. These are perceptions and separate survey questions, not an objective failure rate. Ask for a recent decision influenced by the risk process. Avoid turning the contrast into a causal or paired statistical test. International research motivates the local diagnostic question; it does not measure Kemenkeu. For a ministry, apply the question to public-service objective delivery rather than market competition.

slides.title: The SIGNAL model
slides.note: Introduce the next section: The SIGNAL model. How does a signal become an accountable action?

slides.title: SIGNAL: from evidence to action
slides.note: SIGNAL is our seminar working model: Sense sources, Interpret relevance, Guide the owner, Navigate through human judgment, Act through an owned response, and Learn from effectiveness. A white canvas and six colored arrow segments surround shared objectives, targets, risks and tolerance. The selected phase has a separate explanation panel; no modal obscures the cycle. The cycle advances every 14 seconds. Click or keyboard-select a phase to hold it; Play cycle resumes. Explore the method expands comprehensive details inline and holds playback. AI supports capture, screening and assistance; people remain accountable for all decisions. This workshop demonstrates transparent rules rather than a connected language model. Scores do not predict KPI percentages; projected protection is separate from current risk.

slides.title: Lead the decision
slides.note: Introduce the next section: Lead the decision. You lead the organization. You make the next decision.

slides.title: One organization. Two signal streams. A complete decision cycle.
slides.note: Invite participants to act as the organization leader. First examine risks and initial mitigation commitments, then activate news sources. Work one guided news item together before the independent review. Participants can reject a signal, retain a score, or customize a response with reasons. We then repeat with internal sources. Dashboard closes the loop. Participants use phones or computers; presenter uses separate admin controls.

slides.title: Join the session
slides.note: Presenter opens /admin in the same browser, creates a session, and pastes its LAN audience link here. All phones must reach the laptop. Participants need no account. If setup overruns, shorten the batch debrief rather than the first end-to-end decision.

slides.title: Which organization will you lead?
slides.note: These are fictional Indonesian organizations with strategic exposure. Logistics: export growth, corridor diversification and hub investment. Seafood exporter: export competitiveness and market concentration. Digital: AI differentiation, funded enterprise demand and regulated-market entry. All revenue weights and targets are exercise assumptions. Each objective has two supplied risks. Participants can rename their company and use random-fill aids.

slides.title: The risk and the response are already connected
slides.note: Guide participants through all three menus. Initial risk scores, controls, owners, and plans are supplied. Risk Monitoring uses risk rows with expandable detail; mitigation plans have deadlines. Risk Trigger offers publisher activation. Source changes affect future unreleased batches. The shared guided item is shown to all.

slides.title: A trade-policy shock. Which growth plans are exposed?
slides.note: Show the original headline and opening article paragraphs side by side. Ask which strategic assumptions need review. This is the 2 April announcement as reported 3 April, replayed with an 8 April knowledge cutoff. Verify product coverage, timing, contracts and customers. Do not assume 32% equals a company revenue loss or applies to freight services. These are cropped screenshots of the original webpage, not a reconstructed article.

slides.title: Which organization is affected by this news?
slides.note: Ask the audience before reveal. Export logistics has indirect customer-demand exposure; the seafood exporter has potential goods-market exposure, subject to product and contract checks. Domestic software has no established direct goods-tariff dependency. The first growth objective supports the 12 ? 16 worked example. Hub investment and export concentration can also be linked, with different starting scores. The organization profile and selected objective drive relevance.

slides.title: The alert reaches your risk. You decide whether to capture it.
slides.note: Presenter releases Guided case in /admin. Participants open the new signal in Risk Monitoring, read the source, and approve or decline suggested links; capture notes are optional. Capturing does not change the risk score. For digital participants, a justified neglect is the expected valid contrast.

slides.title: A changed assumption can move the assessment
slides.note: For confirmed export-demand dependence without a revalidated downside growth case, consider likelihood 3→4, impact 4 unchanged. This is an illustrative ordinal assessment, not a probability or Kemenkeu official risk matrix. The source alone does not prove a missed target. Open the risk accordion and choose Keep or Update explicitly.

slides.title: The action follows the exposed dependency
slides.note: After recording the assessment, participants open the suggested response and save a mitigation plan. Multiple plans can be saved. The suggestion is a starting point. Its proposed effect must have a credible link to the dependency. No action is automatically approved by the presenter.

slides.title: Approval creates a commitment. Effectiveness needs evidence.
slides.note: Move the slider to explore 0.5-point mitigation effects. Projection is not measured current risk. Plan approval/completion alone cannot reduce current assessment. Implementation evidence can be captured for a subsequent owner review. Do not convert risk scores into predicted KPI achievement percentages.

slides.title: The dashboard shows decisions and commitments
slides.note: Show the outcome of the first guided case before releasing the wider batch. Do not wait for the room to finish or run a group debrief. Display real aggregate progress if useful in the presenter browser. Same-origin /presentation/deck/ allows authenticated owner-only reads. Participant dashboards show current exposure, plans and history, with KPI actuals marked not supplied. Counts do not measure decision quality or achieved performance improvement.

slides.title: More signals. Better risk decisions.
slides.note: Release the wider External and Internal evidence batches from the presenter view and confirm publication before saying the signals are available. Invite participants to keep role-playing as the risk manager while the presentation continues. They may capture or neglect evidence, retain or revise an assessment, and choose a response; no completion gate or waiting period is needed. Explain the intended value of SIGNAL: dynamic assessments, timely response, shared objective/risk context and accountable human decisions. These are design benefits, not measured proof of improved outcomes. Segue to SPIT as Kemenkeu's institutional direction for integrated control and effective early warning. The next section distinguishes SPIT from its information-system support, SIPT, then explains RP and CMCA. Do not imply SPIT has adopted the SIGNAL brand or that every AI integration is already live.

slides.title: Integrated Internal Control Framework (SPIT)
slides.note: Original standard framework exported directly from the presenter-supplied Framework SPIT.pptx using PowerPoint. Preserve all original labels and layout. Explain the foundation, proactive first line, integrated UKI and Itjen oversight, and system-supported real-time assurance. The application landscape includes Assurance Intelligence System, e-Profiling, CMCA, Risk Platform, Audit Management System and Integrity Platform. Next, focus on RP and CMCA as part of SIPT.

slides.title: One risk register. One view of risk.
slides.note: Presenter-supplied direction: RP becomes the single source of the risk register to enable one view of risk. Shared references connect evidence and assurance to objectives, risk owners and assessments. A consolidated view does not remove unit ownership or independent assurance. These are intended information relationships, not assertions about the current database schema or completed integrations.

slides.title: From periodic snapshots to continuous risk evidence
slides.note: Presenter-supplied direction: the shared risk repository enables integrated assurance, with CMCA as a mainstream means to monitor risk events continuously. Monitoring checks remain linked to registered risks. Data quality, check scope and confirmation matter. Project-based assurance remains necessary to investigate causes and evaluate control effectiveness; continuous checks do not replace independent assurance.

slides.title: The review pattern: exception → confirmation → risk decision
slides.note: Conceptual CMCA flow: a risk-linked automated check surfaces an exception. Its data quality, rule scope and source records must be examined, then a responsible owner confirms whether the exception indicates meaningful exposure. Confirmed evidence can support risk reassessment; neither an exception nor confirmation automatically changes a risk score or constitutes an audit conclusion. Interfaces for SIPT and its platforms are outside this presentation.

slides.title: CMCA is one signal stream. Reports and assurance add context.
slides.note: Reports, minutes and audit findings complement CMCA in a shared risk context. Several records may corroborate one event; they do not each justify another score increase. Explain conceptual evidence relationships without showing application interfaces.

slides.title: AI connects the evidence. People own the decision.
slides.note: Target conceptual flow described by the presenter: RP supplies shared objectives, registered risks, owners, assessments and response history. CMCA, internal reports, audit findings and permitted external evidence provide risk-linked signals. AI assists relevance, explanation, prioritization and draft assessment/response suggestions. The accountable owner validates the evidence and approves any assessment or action. Approved changes return to the shared register and inform monitoring. This is an intended architecture, not a claim of completed production AI integration. System interfaces are outside the scope of this presentation.

slides.title: Follow one risk across the information flow
slides.note: This is an illustrative scenario, not an actual Kemenkeu incident, official KPI or production check. Do not invent a deployed indicator, threshold or official risk score. The example shows how one registered risk can receive several kinds of evidence, producing a human-approved decision rather than disconnected reports. Corroborating records should be evaluated together.

slides.title: A warning is effective when it changes a timely decision
slides.note: The DJKN explanation links an effective early-warning system to timely detection, response, current risk profiles and collaboration across the three lines. Here the RP–CMCA–AI flow is the presenter’s intended means to support that direction, not a claim of proven effectiveness. Evaluate whether signals arrive in time, are relevant, reach an owner and lead to verified action. Alert counts alone do not demonstrate better performance.

slides.title: One view of risk. Shared evidence. Owned decisions.
slides.note: Close on the institutional contribution, not a generic 30-day pilot or a second audience waiting period.
